fullText:
WASHINGTON — The talks to end the Iran war had hit a snag.

Vice President JD Vance had flown to Pakistan for negotiations with the Iranians, a sign that the two sides had narrowed their differences and the White House might be poised to announce a breakthrough.

As the marathon April meeting unfolded, though, U.S. negotiators began to worry: It looked like the Iranians were changing the terms of a potential deal. So, during a pause, they phoned Secretary of State Marco Rubio to get a “steer” on what they should do next, an administration official with direct knowledge of the matter said in an interview.

Rubio agreed that they couldn’t accept Iran’s offer, the official said. There would be no deal.

Rubio isn’t the face of the Iran negotiations. He’s kept a discreet public distance as the unpopular war grinds on. Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff are the main protagonists in the push to end both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

The arrangement is an unusual one. Past secretaries of state commanded the spotlight when it came to war and peace. Henry Kissinger won a Nobel Peace Prize in 1973 for negotiating a ceasefire in the Vietnam War during the Nixon administration. John Kerry, in the Obama administration, flew back and forth between Washington and the Middle East as he tried in vain to broker a peace deal between the Israelis and Palestinians.

Still, Rubio has been a hidden hand throughout, helping craft the Trump administration’s strategy while privately advising the officials who play a more public role in the peace talks.

He holds a unique place in the Cabinet, one of the most expansive in the modern presidency. Rubio doubles as national security adviser — first in an acting capacity, now permanent — meaning he has a spacious office in the West Wing and gets more face time with Trump than most Cabinet members.

This account is based on interviews with 12 present and former administration officials and others close to Rubio and the White House. Many spoke on condition of anonymity to talk freely about internal policy and political dynamics.

“The reason that the American people perhaps don’t see Secretary Rubio as front and center on Iran is because he really does have the rest of the world to worry about and pays enormous attention to the Western Hemisphere and our European allies,” White House chief of staff Susie Wiles told NBC News. “President Trump is so busy and active around the world, it takes more than one person. So, Secretary Rubio is leading the other efforts around the world that are so important to America’s stability and future promise.”

Trump has given Rubio wide latitude, allowing America’s top diplomat to be selective when it comes to the public parts of the job. Rubio was more visible in the early phase of the Iran war than in the later stages. That could prove advantageous down the road.

Polls show widespread American disenchantment with the conflict. As public opinion hardens, Rubio may be better positioned to sidestep any political backlash than Vance, who has attended futile rounds of peace talks in far-flung locales.

Rubio has said publicly that he currently has no plans to run in 2028, and two people familiar with the matter have told NBC News he has also said that privately. He has acknowledged behind closed doors that the landscape may be tough for Republicans in 2028 and suggested that a presidential run in 2032 or 2036 may be more promising, a person close to him said.

But Rubio’s comments don’t close the door completely. A second person close to him said that he has not ruled out a potential 2028 presidential run, but he is not discussing his future plans.

“Nobody knows what he’s going to do,” the source said. “Political calculation does not factor into literally anything that he’s doing right now.”

Another consideration is personal. Rubio has also said privately that after nearly three decades in public office he may want to take a job in the private sector when Trump’s term ends, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.

His financial disclosure form shows his net worth to be no more than $240,000 apart from his house, listed in a range between $1 million and $5 million. Those are modest sums in an administration packed with officials worth $100 million or more.

Rubio could readily land a lucrative job that would be a boon to himself, his wife and their four children if he sat out the race, and at 55, he is young enough to mount a campaign later on.

Once angry rivals, Rubio and Trump have developed a good rapport. Rubio may be in and out of the Oval Office five or six times a day, a White House official told NBC News. Both love sports, and they’ve been overheard jawing about baseball batting averages or a knockout punch in the latest mixed martial arts match, the official said.

Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a prepared statement: “As President Trump says, Marco Rubio will go down as one of the greatest Secretaries of State in history. The president and Secretary Rubio have successfully restored American dominance on the world stage and are relentlessly working to advance our foreign policy interests.”

After spending 14 years in the Senate, Rubio grasps the politics and legislative tactics needed to pass bills into law and will advise the president on ways to push his agenda through Congress, the official said.

“I can think of many times in which we’re talking about whatever he [Trump] is focused on that day and he’ll say, ‘What do you think, Marco?’ I’ve heard that more times than I can count,” a person close to the White House said. “They jell well together. I’ve seen people who don’t jell well with the president, and Marco is not one of those people.”

Rubio’s influence in the peace talks is largely behind the scenes. Witkoff checks in with him before agreeing to attend negotiating sessions, takes guidance before meetings and briefs him afterward, the administration official said.

Last weekend, the two men spoke by phone multiple times about an escalating conflict involving Iran and Yemen. On Saturday, Witkoff reached Rubio while the secretary of state was at the University of Florida football stadium in Gainesville, watching his son play for the Gators, the official said.

Leaving the Senate last year to work for Trump was a gamble for Rubio. The two faced off in the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, where they one-upped each other in schoolyard taunts. Trump derided the Florida lawmaker as “Little Marco.” Rubio mocked the New York businessman’s hand size.

Time and pragmatic politics have transformed the rivalry into a partnership. The Senate confirmed Rubio by a vote of 99-0, a feat that has impressed even Trump.

“It’s not an easy job to be both the secretary of state and the national security adviser, but Secretary Rubio has managed it beautifully,” Wiles said. “He is an experienced, smart and intuitive adviser to the president and the rest of the team, be it national security or foreign affairs.”

Other Cabinet secretaries have flamed out since Trump began his second term. Attorney General Pam Bondi is gone, as are Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard.

Rubio, by contrast, has thrived in a job that aligns with his political and policy interests. One of his main priorities is building American clout in the Western Hemisphere, where he is leaving an imprint.

He helped forge an oil deal with Venezuela this summer that the Trump administration believes will buoy both the U.S. and Venezuelan economies.

Earlier this month, Rubio met with heads of state in Latin America as he sought to combat illegal immigration and drug trafficking.

The son of Cuban émigrés, he is also driving the administration’s effort to transform Cuba and bring an end to the regime in Havana.

If he can nudge Venezuela and Cuba toward democratic governance, that could be an enviable legacy for a secretary of state who is nursing presidential ambitions.

Rubio’s statement to a Colombian radio station earlier this month that he currently has “no plans” to mount another campaign was not a hard-and-fast denial. Even if it was, it might not matter. When Rubio first ran for president, he made clear he was done with the Senate. And he sounded adamant.

“I have only said like 10000 times I will be a private citizen in January,” he wrote on social media in May 2016, two months after he dropped out of the presidential contest. The following month, he did an about-face, ran for re-election and won.

If Vance enters the race and falters in the Republican primaries, Rubio might jump in the contest, the second person close to Rubio said.

Another possibility would be for Rubio to become Vance’s running mate, something he would be inclined to do if asked, this person said. Trump himself has suggested the two men pair up in 2028, and his opinion counts given his grip on the Republican base.

Trump likes to ask people privately who they think should be the GOP nominee.

“Whoever the Republican nominee is in 2028, Donald Trump will decide,” the White House official said. “Of course, the primary process will run. But the president will have such an outsized influence in it, and I think he does wish they would run together.”

After the midterm elections in November, attention will turn to 2028 and the post-Trump era. Rubio won’t have much time to decide his future.

“If he’s serious about running, he would have to say so reasonably soon,” the White House official said. “Once you’re elected, you never really get rid of that bug. Ultimately, if there’s an opportunity and an opening, you’d be almost fighting your instincts not to do it.”

title: Six-time Grand Slam champion Salisbury retires
description: Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury retires from professional tennis.
fullText:
Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury has retired from professional tennis.

Londoner Salisbury chose this month's US Open as his final event and reached the semi-finals with his long-time partner Rajeev Ram, who had also decided to retire.

The venue was fitting, as in 2023 Salisbury and Ram became the first pair in history to win three consecutive US Open men's doubles titles.

Salisbury is Britain's most successful men's doubles player of the Open era. He also won the 2020 Australian Open with Ram, and two mixed doubles titles with Desirae Krawczyk.

The 34-year-old says he has been thinking about his future for a while, and is now "very happy with the decision".

"Tennis has been my life for as long as I can remember and I have been incredibly fortunate to have had all the opportunities, experiences and success that I have," he posted on Instagram.

"To be able to travel the world and call playing tennis my job has been a dream come true and I never believed I could have lived the life and had the career that I have.

"I gave it my all and know I can be proud and look back with no regrets."

Salisbury took a three-month break at the start of this year, having told BBC Sport about the anxiety which had been affecting him on tour.

While he did not think it affected his tennis very much, he said it left him with a "feeling of dread" which made life on the road far less enjoyable.

"I had some time off for a few months earlier on in the year - I wasn't really enjoying being on tour for a few reasons," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I came back and I didn't really have a successful year. Then I teamed back up with my partner, Rajeev Ram, who I had all my success in Grand Slam titles [with] so it was great playing with him again and he was retiring at the US Open this year.

"I thought I could go on [until the] end of this year, maybe next year but I felt like it was nice to finish my career playing with him at the US Open where we had our success, and we had a good run making the semi-finals to finish."

Salisbury finishes his career with 17 tour level titles, including the season-ending ATP Finals of 2022 and 2023.

title: Champion Van Gerwen loses in first round to Gurney
description: Defending champion Michael van Gerwen falls to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney in the opening round of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
fullText:
Defending champion Michael van Gerwen fell to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney in the opening round of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.

Northern Ireland's Gurney raced into a 3-0 lead before the Dutch top seed reeled off five consecutive legs to put himself on the brink of victory.

However, Gurney, who was drafted in as a late replacement when Lourence Ilagan withdrew from the 32-man field, responded by taking the ninth leg.

And when Van Gerwen missed six match darts, he was able to level the match at 5-5 and win the decider with the throw.

Gurney will now take on England's Ross Smith in the last 16 on Saturday after he advanced past Kevin Doets 6-3.

World number one Luke Littler will get under way on Friday against former UK Open champion Danny Noppert, having recently whitewashed the Dutchman 6-0 on his way to winning the Czech Darts Open.

World number two Luke Humphries also emerged victorious in another England versus Netherlands encounter, progressing 6-4 against Jermaine Wattimena.

Dutch number one Gian van Veen gained a measure of revenge for the home fans with a 6-2 triumph over Chris Dobey.

Dirk van Duijvenbode fought back from 4-1 down to defeat Sweden's Viktor Tingstrom 6-4, while Ryan Searle threw four 180s as he dispatched former world champion Rob Cross 6-2.

Searle goes on to play Josh Rock, who won the last three legs to edge out Stephen Bunting 6-5.

Karel Sedlacek marked his debut at the tournament with a 6-4 win over New Zealander Ben Robb and will take on Van Veen next.

description: The Jays are in the thick of a slapstick caper of a wildcard race, but with today being an off day I thought I’d look at the minor leagues as their seasons wrap up. The International League (AAA) goes through this weekend, so the Buffalo Bisons have a few more to play, but the other […]
fullText:
The Jays are in the thick of a slapstick caper of a wildcard race, but with today being an off day I thought I'd look at the minor leagues as their seasons wrap up. The International League (AAA) goes through this weekend, so the Buffalo Bisons have a few more to play, but the other levels' seasons came to a close over the course of the last couple of weeks.

The Vancouver Canadians won the Northwest League championship in a 12 inning thriller on Friday night. You can read a full recap here, but it involved a three run comeback in the ninth to force extras and plenty of other drama. It's the Canadians' sixth league championship since they became a Blue Jays affiliate in 2011, and their second since the Northwest League was converted from short season ball to A+ in the minor league reorganization.

As Tom mentioned in his roundup yesterday, the rosters for the Arizona Fall League were released. The AFL is a developmental league that is mostly used to give prospects who missed time or otherwise need a little more work an opportunity for some additional reps. This year, it runs from October 3rd through November 14th. Because the number of players teams want to send is limited, especially on the pitching side, AFL rosters are blended. The Jays team up with the Cubs, A's, Red Sox and Angels to form the Mesa Solar Sox.

Participation in the AFL can be a big opportunity for prospects. They get a chance to shine when there aren't any other minor leagues going, with scouts from all 30 teams paying attention. Recent proof is Spencer Miles, who caught the Jays' attention with 8.2 impressive innings in last year's AFL.

The Jays prospects going this year are:

Brandon Barriera: The 2022 first round pick has alternated between injured and ineffective so far in his career. This season was more of the same, as he managed just 38.2 innings but walked 29 in that span. He's managed just 66 innings over four pro seasons, so the Jays are likely both inclined to get him more action and not too concerned with sheltering him anymore.

Gilberto Batista: It was a rough year for Batista. He recorded a 7.86 ERA across 87 innings as a multi-inning reliever for Vancouver. He did show some promise last year with Dunedin, after being acquired from the Red Sox in the Danny Jansen trade.

Jake Bloss: Bloss is the exciting name from a Jays fan point of view. He came back from Tommy John surgery throwing 2mph harder than he had before the surgery, but then went down almost immediately with a teres major strain. If he can make a few healthy appearances, retain the stuff bump, and continue to rediscover his command after the surgery, he'll be set up for a potential rotation role with the big league club next year.

Fernando Perez: The word for Perez' season is mysterious. He ranked high on our prospect list last winter on the strength of his elite command and strong results across A+ Vancouver and AA New Hampshire, but had a disastrous start to his 2026, walking 10 in nine innings over his first three starts. He was placed on the Development List, a new addition to the minors since the 2021 reorganization that basically allows teams to take players off the roster indefinitely to manage workloads or to work on things outside of game action. He returned for three more appearances in August and September and didn't look any better. Command is Perez' whole draw as a prospect, so losing it so completely is concerning. The AFL will be a big opportunity to show that he's righted the ship. He's Rule 5 eligible, and coming into the season I'd have expected him to warrant protection, but that seems a distant concern now.

Yondrei Rojas: Our #32 prospect entering the season, Rojas struggled to build on his strong 2025 this year. He struck out just 20% of batters, mostly at AA, and missed fewer bats that last season. He's 23 and Rule 5 eligible, so this might be one more chance to harness his plus fastball-slider combination and mark himself as a future Blue Jays bullpen hand.

Aaron Parker: 2026 was a breakout for the third year pro. He cut down his swing rate and went on a power binge at New Hampshire, launching 19 home runs in 87 games. He's a below average defensive catcher and his 67% contact rate is scary, but plus power is plus power, and he may have a shot at the third catcher role at some point in 2027.

Jake Casey: The Kent State prospect has just hit since the Jays took him in the 15th round last year. This season, a broken hamate wiped out his first couple of months, but he managed 13 home runs in just 64 games. He still needs to show he can adjust to upper minors quality spin, and the results are iffy so far, but as long as he keeps producing he'll warrant watching.

Jake Cook: Last year's third rounder was just average in A ball, which would be concerning for most pedigreed college draftees. Cook is just two years into switching back to the field from the mound, though, and working to overhaul the pure slap, inside-out swing he used in college to try to develop a modicum of power. He did up his home run total over last year, from 3 to 5, in spite of switching to wood bats and facing better pitching, and he improved as the year went on. He was also 22 for 27 stealing bases, showcasing the athletic tools that convinced the Jays to gamble a top 100 pick on him. He needs reps, and the AFL will offer an opportunity against pitching a bit better than he's seen so far.

Because they share a team with the Angels, the Jay's prospects will get a chance to catch up with Arjun Nimmala. He finished the season red hot, clubbing four home runs and four doubles last week for the AA Rocket City Trash Pandas.

Baseball America has graded the year for each farm system. They give the Jays a B+ overall, which seems about right to me. When I reviewed the performance of the top 40 before the deadline, there were a lot of guys moving in different directions, but the overall trend seemed to be upwards.

There were several impressive breakouts, although many of those guys will miss next year's list because they've already graduated. Miles, Brandon Valenzuela, and Brett Bateman have all already far exceeded their prospect expectations. Valenzuela has fallen off badly in the second half and Bateman is surely playing over his head offensively, but both still project as at least quality role players now. For Miles, his peripheral stats fully support his exceptional performance this year, and continued health seems like the only real question. Still on the farm is Nolan Perry, who returned from Tommy John and immediately torched three levels, striking out 117 in only 82.2 innings. Sean Keys, who raced through AA and AAA early in the season, is in between. He's with the Jays right now but not seeing a lot of playing time. His early MLB results haven't been good, but the underlying contact and power data remain tantalizing.

Of course, there were some disappointments as well. Bloss showcased improved stuff in his own TJ comeback, but remained healthy only briefly. Juan Sanchez, last year's Dominican Summer League star, has so far failed to consistently translate his success in the US. Ricky Tiedemann, among others, continued to struggle with his health.

The farm's ranking, in BA's reckoning, rose from 17 to 15 between the preseason and the midseason update. That's impressive given that a lot of the preseason value was tied to Trey Yesavage, who graduated soon after returning from his early season shoulder issues. They might dip slightly this winter, as they traded top prospect Arjun Nimmala and had fewer resources in the draft than most other teams, but the system produced new talent, fed the major league team, and allowed them to make major deadline acquisitions without moving backwards in overall talent. That's a good year.

title: Abhishek hits fastest century in full-member T20s
description: Abhishek Sharma hits a 30-ball century - the fastest in a T20 international between two full-member nations - in India's third T20 against Afghanistan.
fullText:
India 221-7 (20 overs): Abhishek 108 (34), Samson 50 (35); Omarzai 2-27

Afghanistan 94 (14.1 overs): Zadran 25 (16); Bishnoi 3-26

Abhishek Sharma hit a 30-ball century - the fastest in a T20 international between two full-member nations - in India's 127-run victory in the third T20 against Afghanistan in Delhi.

Opener Abhishek, who was knocked off the top of the T20 batting rankings in July, continued to make 108 from 34 balls, hitting nine fours and 11 sixes in India's 221-7.

The 26-year-old reached three figures in the ninth over - at that stage India were 132-0 - having scored a remarkable 96 of his 100 runs in boundaries.

The only exceptions were the single to get to his hundred, another in the previous over and a two in the third.

It was Abhishek's third T20 international ton and the 10th of his entire T20 career.

And while it beat the previous fastest century for a full-member nation - a 33-ball effort by New Zealand's Finn Allen against South Africa at this year's T20 World Cup - it was not even Abhishek's quickest in the format.

The thrilling left-hander hit a 28-ball ton for Punjab against Meghalaya in Indian domestic cricket in 2024.

Against Afghanistan, he dominated Afghanistan's pace bowlers with his pull shot and powered the spinners down the ground.

He helped India take 100 from the powerplay but, after he was caught behind off the bowling of Rashid Khan, the hosts added 79 in the remaining 10.1 overs.

Afghanistan collapsed to 94 in response, giving the hosts a 3-0 series clean sweep.

title: Saudi Arabia dropped from World Rally Championship
description: The final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship will be held in Italy instead of Saudi Arabia because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.
fullText:
The final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship (WRC) will be held in Italy instead of Saudi Arabia because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia had been set to host the 14th and final rally of the season from 11-14 November.

The championship has now been shortened to 13 rounds and will conclude with the Rally Italia in Sardinia from 1-4 October.

Rally Saudi Arabia in Jeddah, which joined the WRC calendar in 2025, will still take place on the planned dates but as part of the Middle East Rally Championship.

The FIA, the global governing body for motor sports, said Saudi Arabia "remained ready to host the event safely" but the decision was due to "ongoing uncertainty in the region and its effect on logistical arrangements".

Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca

In a statement, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "We have worked closely with our partners to explore every possible route that would allow Rally Saudi Arabia to take place as planned.

"These are never easy decisions, particularly after the significant work undertaken by everyone involved in preparing for the event.

"While the WRC element of the event will not take place this year, our confidence in the organisers and in the long-term future of the rally remains unchanged."

Great Britain's Elfyn Evans sits at the top of the WRC standings before the final round, 17 points clear of Finland's Sami Pajari, and is the favourite to take the title with a maximum of 35 points up for grabs across the final round.

The Welshman has finished runner-up in the championship five times, and is looking to join former British winners Colin McRae and Richard Burns in winning the title.

Numerous conflicts are ongoing in the Middle East, including the Israel-Gaza war, with Israel and the United States at war with Iran and Saudi Arabia battling Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The WRC is not the first sporting event to avoid the region, with the FIA cancelling Formula One Grand Prix races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April.

The Bahrain race has since been relocated to Malaysia - to be staged in early October - with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi later in the season are scheduled to go ahead as planned.

In February, tennis players, staff and media were left stranded in Dubai following missile strikes on the United Arab Emirates while in March, an ATP Challenger event in the country was disrupted by drone strikes. The sport's governing bodies are reportedly considering replacement hosts for events in the region for the 2027 season.

On Wednesday, English golfer Matt Fitzpatrick said he is not "100% comfortable" with prospect of travelling to Dubai for his DP World Tour Championship title defence in November.

title: The big questions for Tuchel's first England squad since World Cup
description: Before Thomas Tuchel names his first squad since the World Cup on Friday, BBC Sport looks at the big questions facing the England boss.
fullText:
Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday.

While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs.

Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like.

Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play?

BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel.

Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut.

Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach.

He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo.

But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back.

Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party.

It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton pair Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Jarrad Branthwaite are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list.

Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup.

That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players.

Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury.

Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico

FA to canvass England players in World Cup review

Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won.

Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month.

Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United.

This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa.

John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play.

Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad.

What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July.

John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings.

In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel.

But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions.

These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup.

Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men.

But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame.

Away from the height of those emotions in July, the Football Association is completing a review into England's World Cup campaign. The FA has been keen to stress that this assessment is a standard process, rather than an indication of wider concern or alarm about England's third-place finish.

Indeed, key figures at the FA view the tournament in which England achieved their best finish since 1966 as a success, and the organisation has already backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.

Tuchel and members of his backroom team gave their contributions to the review at St George's Park in late August. England players' opinions are also being gathered before a report is presented to senior bosses at the FA.

The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament. After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.

The content of the review won't be made public, but the next three weeks will give an indication of whether the camp is still as together as that night at the Azteca.

title: Trump's rate hike comments place renewed scrutiny on the Fed's independence
description:
President Donald Trump with Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh at the White House in Washington, DC, on May 22. - Jonathan Ernst/Reuters/File

The Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years has ushered in a new twist to the already unusual relationship between President Donald Trump and the world’s most powerful central bank.

Trump raised eyebrows on Wednesday evening by appearing to suggest that he gave Kevin Warsh, his handpicked Fed chairman, permission to raise rates – even though it was the “wrong” move. The president implied that Warsh had no choice but to embrace a rate increase because the Fed chief was outnumbered on the “hostile” rate-setting committee he oversees.

“I talked to Kevin and I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter…I said, ‘Do what you want because it doesn’t matter’ because he doesn’t have the votes,” Trump told reporters.

The remarks raise plenty of questions about how much – if at all – Warsh is consulting with a president who has been willing to cross red lines in his quest for dramatically lower interest rates.

Those questions are especially sensitive because the Fed is designed to be insulated from the political winds in Washington. Central bankers are required to make trillion-dollar decisions on whether to raise or lower interest rates based on what’s best for the economy, not for the political party in power.

Tellingly, some Fed watchers and former officials reacted to the remarks with disbelief.

“It’s an unusual and unfortunate comment to make. Clearly, the Fed chair does not need the president’s permission to raise rates,” Eric Rosengren, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, told CNN on Thursday. “The implication is that the chair got a hall pass. I have no idea how truthful the comment was.”

Krishna Guha, vice chairman and head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI who criticized Warsh’s initial stumbles, dismissed Trump’s claims.

“The market believes – and with good grounds – that Kevin Warsh owned this decision and that the committee was strongly united behind him,” Guha said. “There is no evidence here or to the market at large that Warsh was dragged into this by colleagues – or permissioned by the president.”

The risk is that Trump fuels suspicions that swirled on Wall Street this summer that Warsh may not be truly independent. That’s dangerous because a Fed doing the White House’s bidding could lose control of market-set interest rates, dramatically increasing the cost of mortgages and car loans. And a loss of faith in Fed independence could unhinge inflation expectations among investors and consumers.

The Fed declined to comment to CNN about Trump’s remarks.

For his part, Warsh tap-danced around questions related to the man who nominated him.

“I’m not a Wall Street newsletter. Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street,” Warsh said during the press conference on Wednesday. “We’ll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them.”

Asked by a reporter when he last spoke with the president, Warsh said: “I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president.”

Tim Mahedy, CEO and chief economist at research firm Access/Macro, said he found that response from Warsh “strange.”

“The right answer is, ‘I didn’t talk to the president.’ I don’t think the president is talking to Warsh beforehand. That would be shocking,” said Mahedy, a former official at the IMF and San Francisco Fed.

The other risk is that, intentionally or not, Trump diminishes Warsh as an ineffectual leader – just as he appeared to be starting to find his footing.

“It makes it seem like Warsh has no control over this committee, like he was completely ineffectual in convincing his colleagues,” said Mahedy.

Warsh emerged from the meeting looking independent. Not only did he preside over a rate hike the White House did not want, but he explained it clearly and with the unanimous support of his colleagues – including former Fed Chair Jerome Powell.

“It felt like the day the Fed became Warsh’s Fed,” Evercore’s Guha said. “He was a lot more assured, coherent and credible yesterday. What he’s saying basically adds up.”

But now if Warsh and a majority of his colleagues on the committee decide against a rate hike, he will face questions about whether the president put his finger on the scale.

In the past, most presidents have gone out of their way to even avoid the appearance of interfering with the Fed because it was widely accepted that an independent Fed builds confidence.

None of this is to say Trump unleashed on the Fed in a way that would have unnerved investors. In fact, Trump’s initial reaction to the first rate hike under Warsh was relatively mild, especially compared with his relentless and deeply personal condemnation of Powell, his last handpicked Fed chair.

While Trump bashed Warsh’s colleagues as “very hostile” and “very political,” he singled out the Fed chief for praise. “He’s a good man, Kevin Warsh,” Trump said.

“People were fearful of a fierce backlash from the president against this decision to raise rates and a resumption of the conflict between the White House and the Fed,” Guha said.

Of course, the Warsh-Trump relationship will continue to evolve, likely guided by what happens next to inflation, borrowing costs and the path of the S&P 500 and all-important Treasury rates.

Mahedy said he worries that the relationship will break down if the Warsh-led Fed continues to raise rates – as many suspect it will be forced to.

“It’s not hard to see more blame being put on the Fed and Warsh – and then it will start to look a lot like Powell,” said Mahedy. “It’s kind of a train wreck – but a slow-moving one.”

title: U.N.-backed experts cite possible U.S. war crimes in Iran strikes
description:
— Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.’s top human rights body say they have found “reasonable grounds” to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran’s theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.
The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.
fullText:
GENEVA (AP) — Human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.'s top human rights body say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. They also accuse Iran's theocratic government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its own people in a report published Thursday.

The report, while not binding, adds to international evidence gathered about crimes in the war in Iran, and could eventually be used in efforts to reach justice in international courts.

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the U.N.'s top human rights body, which is based in Geneva.

The experts were expected to present their findings on Monday to the council, which is made up of 47 U.N. member countries.

The international fact-finding mission says its findings on U.S. war crimes center on a pair of U.S. airstrikes that killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children.

At the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February, at least one U.S. missile hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, according to an Associated Press investigation. There has been no final accounting of what happened.

Iranian state media have said 168 people were killed in the strike, most of them children.

"Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," a U.N. statement about the team's findings said.

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press seeking comment.

In their report, the experts concluded that "the building of the school was the intended point of impact" and the resulting damage wasn't the result of an errant strike or collateral damage from an attack on a compound of Iran's Revolutionary Guard next to the school.

The Trump administration has yet to directly accept responsibility or release the findings of a Pentagon investigation into the school bombing.

The U.N.-backed team based its allegations on two strikes — one involving Tomahawk missiles that hit the "clearly identifiable" school, and another in which Precision Strike Missiles dispersed tungsten pellets over a "clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area" in the southern city of Lamerd, also on Feb. 28.

The U.N.-backed team said 22 civilian men and women were killed. U.S. Central Command has denied responsibility for the strike on Lamerd.

The team found that killings by state security forces in Iran have occurred on a "staggering scale," and civilians faced "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government."

Iranian security forces carried out "violent repression" over the last two years by firing assault rifles into crowds, beating protesters and arresting healthcare workers, among other things, the team said. Detainees faced torture, and were deprived of legal counsel, leaving their families "in the dark" about their whereabouts, the experts said.

The Tehran government intensified the use of the death penalty, and said more than 70 people – including five women and three boys – remain at "imminent risk of execution," they added.

"The report concluded that many of these gross violations amount to crimes against humanity — including murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians," the statement said.

The experts said the United States and Iran should halt all rights violations and crimes, and provide "full reparations to victims."

The report, built on a "victims-centered approach," was based on interviews with 73 people both inside and outside Iran, along with documentation, satellite imagery, photographic and video material and information from "credible" organizations and experts, the experts wrote.

The ongoing conflict that has driven people from their homes in Iran as well as an internet shutdown and a lack of full cooperation from the two governments partially impeded the team's efforts to get information.

Nearly three dozen requests from the experts for information from Iran's government went unanswered, they said, as have requests in June to the U.S. government for information and meetings with officials.

fullText:
Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces

The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.

The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.

The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.

“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.

“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”

Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.

Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.

A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.

The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.

In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.

The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.

Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.

“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.

“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.

Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.

“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.

Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.

The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.

Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.

“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.

Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

title: FA chair demands Infantino release World Cup sell-off documents
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup in a letter sent by Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt.

Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.

Infantino should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October.

The letter, also sent to Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, makes accusations of failures in governance and a breakdown in culture within the world football governing body.

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

The proposal was scrapped following widespread opposition from national associations.

Hewitt's letter adds that there should be an independent review of how FFE was conceived, by whom, and how the private investment was put to tender.

Last month, Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at three US courts over the FFE plan, demanded the release of all documents.

Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.

Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

The Football Association was troubled by the Balogun situation from the outset, and had requested the release of the documents relating to his overturned ban during the World Cup.

Forward Balogun, 25, was allowed to play against Belgium in the last 16 when he would have expected to be serving a one-match suspension.

The striker had been shown a straight red card for a foul on defender Tarik Muharemovic in the 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last 32.

Fifa then said the automatic one-match ban would be suspended for a year. No reasoning behind the move was provided, beyond citing a rule which allows punishments to be suspended.

The FA, which had sent a letter of support for Infantino's re-election before the Balogun incident, had deep concerns about political intervention.

US President Donald Trump later confirmed he called Infantino asking for Balogun's ban to be reviewed.

Then the FFE proposal, revealed through the media just days after the World Cup final, fractured the game.

Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation last month.

Many national associations, including those of England, Wales and Scotland, have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino's re-election.

But Infantino still holds a great deal of support around the globe, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania reiterating their backing.

After FFE was cancelled, Infantino called a meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Morocco.

But as yet there has been no contact with the Fifa Council to explain the controversial plan.

That is set to change next month when Infantino must face Hewitt and the other 35 Fifa Council members.

fullText:
STRASBOURG, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Canada and Europe should ally to protect their markets, democracies and rule of law in a world dominated by the United States and China, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after an EU ‌proposal to make Canada an "associate member".

The Canadian prime minister received warm applause for his speech to the European Parliament, delivered hours after U.S. President Donald ‌Trump threatened trade sanctions in response to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to create a new status for the EU-Canada relationship.

Carney did not adopt the term "associate member" used a day earlier ​by von der Leyen, but said he appreciated "the ambition" that her suggestion conveyed.

"Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together," Carney said.

He was not seeking to form a "third bloc" to act as "a great-power rival" to Washington and Beijing "only with better manners," Carney said in a line that drew laughs.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience, so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, ‌our democracies, our rule of law."

He told reporters after the ⁠speech that it would be up to the EU how it proposed to describe any future relationship, and that the substance of any agreement would be more important than the name given to it.

Trump threatened late on Wednesday to take action against the ⁠EU if it moved forward with von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an 'associate member' of the bloc.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, calling the proposal "laughable".

"If it's a good ​intention, ​that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.

The ​European Commission said von der Leyen's proposal — which had yet ‌to be fleshed out and would need to be approved by EU member states to go forward — was not a hostile act.

"As our President (von der Leyen) made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.

Asked about Trump's threats, Carney told reporters: "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally."

title: Phillies can't live in fear of another playoff bullpen debacle
description: Phillies' World Series hopes hinge on this group after three straight October disasters.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — There are 12 former All-Stars and at least two future Hall of Famers occupying the Philadelphia Phillies clubhouse on a given day. This collection of well-paid, salty, accomplished stars will command most of the attention as the Phillies attempt, for the fifth consecutive year, to bring a World Series title home to Philly.

Then there is Jonathan Bowlan, an easygoing dude from Memphis, quiet and forthright, making his way through his first full season in the big leagues. Bowlan might not realize it yet, but he may have more to do with whether the Phillies raise a trophy in October than any of the superstars.

Bowlan, 26, has emerged as the Phillies' primary set-up man, aiming, along with 25-year-old Orion Kerkering, to form a bridge between the club's quartet of ace starting pitchers and their dominant closer, Jhoan Duran.

It is thankless work, and the sixth through 10th innings are exactly where the Phillies' prior championship quests have gone awry. Lately, they've been trouble spots as the club staggers down the stretch to finalize a National League wild-card berth.

Bowlan has given up a run in five consecutive appearances entering Wednesday, Sept. 16, including late-game homers in three of those; Kerkering gave up runs in four of his last five games, including multiple-run outings in Phillies losses.

"Those innings," says interim manager Don Mattingly, "are always the stressful innings.

"And you'd like to be able to lock down that end of the game when you get a lead or you're in a close game."

Mattingly was speaking after Bowlan gave up a first-pitch, three-run, pinch-hit homer to Daylen Lile in the seventh inning of a 6-3 loss to Washington, the latest setback that imperiled the club's wild-card standing. Oh, the team's still on fairly firm ground, with a 95% chance to reach the playoffs, according to FanGraphs.

It's just that the Phillies keep slipping down the pecking order and, with a rough combo of a flailing lineup and slumping bullpen, inspiring little confidence in their postseason chances.

For Bowlan, learning to cope has come before having to face the bright lights of the postseason. He's found that in reflecting on failure, there's a fine line between quickly moving on and interrogating what went wrong.

"There's definitely times I lose some sleep at night, for sure," Bowlan tells USA TODAY Sports. "But as soon as you wake up the next morning, it's a new day. It's a blessing. God woke me up to continue on. And you can't live in the past. Because you can learn from your experiences, for sure. And that's what I continue to try and do.

"It's taken some time to learn that, about the short memory. But I've gotten to the point where, 'Yeah, you can think about it a little bit.' And there's times where it was a tough thing to happen in that situation.

"But you live and you learn. All you can do is just keep chugging along. Keep moving."

That ethos certainly applies to the Phillies, who won't glean any sympathy from rival fanbases, given their four-year run of success powered by an aggressive ownership group bent on winning their first World Series since 2008.

Yet every bite at the apple ends rottenly for all but one team every year. And October's late innings have been a long-running soap opera in Philly.

In 2022, it was Jose Alvarado, relieving ace Zack Wheeler in the sixth inning of World Series Game 6, the Phillies leading 1-0, only to give up a left-on-left three-run blast to Yordan Alvarez, enabling the Houston Astros to nail down the championship.

A year later, it was the rookie Kerkering – with just eight major league appearances under his belt – summoned to protect a 1-0 lead in the seventh inning of NLCS Game 3, the Phillies nine outs from seizing a 3-0 lead on the ostensibly overmatched Arizona Diamondbacks.

Instead, Kerkering gave up three consecutive hits, including Lourdes Gurriel's RBI double, to tie the game and set the stage for closer Craig Kimbrel yielding a walk-off hit, one of Kimbrel's many failings in that series. The Diamondbacks won in seven games.

In 2024, the goats were numerous – from Alvarado to Carlos Estevez to Jeff Hoffman, who yielded six earned runs and recorded four outs across three games – as the Mets pulled off a stunning NLDS upset.

And last year, it was Kerkering, aiming to keep the Phillies alive in the 11th inning of NLDS Game 4 at Los Angeles, but infamously fielding Andy Pages' two-out ground ball and throwing home instead of taking an easy out at first.

Now, Kerkering realizes that staying true to himself is just as important in the aftermath as breaking down pitches that backfired or physical errors. And even his recent struggles have provided teachable moments.

"You look at some of those struggles you've gone through the last couple years and just try to learn a lot more," says Kerkering, "since I came up through the system so fast and wasn't able to really go through those downs. I think going through them now a little bit has been super-helpful. You'll go on some great runs and some not-so-fun runs. But that's what baseball is. It's a game of failure.

"You just try to make sure you get back on who you're supposed to be as a person."

Bowlan's recent struggles have overshadowed his excellent work most of this season. He's blown five saves but also has a 1.04 WHIP and struck out 71 in 55 innings.

It's been a startling rise for Bowlan, who admitted he was a bit stunned – "Kind of a whoa moment," he says – when the Phillies acquired him over the winter for longtime lefty reliever Matt Strahm. The Phillies' suggestion he lean more heavily on his four-seam fastball – its usage has risen from 33.6% to 48% - has paid significant dividends.

That will be his best friend come the postseason, waters he's looking forward to navigating.

"I've heard that being in the playoffs is one of the best experiences you can have in this game," says Bowlan. "Being in that situation, from what I've learned, you've got to just slow things down. You can't let things overwhelm you. These guys have been through it. They've been through big situations.

"I'm just trying to learn from them to the best of my ability."

Both Bowlan and Kerkering are operating a rung higher than the Phillies anticipated this season. They signed right-hander Brad Keller to a two-year, $22 million deal over the winter after his stellar 2025 with the Chicago Cubs. But Keller struggled into June, missed a month with forearm tendinitis and then tore the UCL in his throwing elbow in July.

Veteran lefties Alvarado, Brooks Raley and Tim Mayza balance out the bullpen, but aren't necessarily built for one-inning, high-leverage situations.

That's just one reason why Bowlan and Kerkering will be front and center this postseason.

Kerkering is now in his third full major league season, yet maintains he's "still the pup" on a club with 10-year vets like Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Zack Wheeler. He has been through the postseason fire, for better or worse, and knows what he'll tell Bowlan before his October indoctrination.

"Think of it like you're playing the Dodgers, you're playing the Braves' series – (multiply) that by five," says Kerkering. "The intensity, how much people care, how much louder and the passion.

"But you still have to make your pitches. It's a big moment for the pitcher, a big moment for the hitters. It doesn't matter how long they've been there. You're battling each other out and there's very few teams left.

"You're highlighted, basically."

And the spotlight is about to get a lot brighter.

title: Why EFL matches get postponed for international call-ups
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team explains why some League One and League two matches get postponed due to international call-ups.
fullText:
Matches in League One and League Two can be postponed during international breaks due to players being selected for international matches.

The English Football League (EFL) allows clubs to postpone fixtures should they receive a sufficient number of call-ups.

At least three of players have to be selected for their country's senior, under-21, under-20 or under-19 sides in order to request a postponement.

Players who are named on international standby lists or long lists will not count towards the three players at the time of announcement.

International age group players only qualify if they have been named in the starting XI, or been a named substitute making an appearance prior to the 75th minute, in either:

50% of a club's first-team matches

four of the last five first-team matches

If a player is signed by a club in either late August or during the January transfer window and they then get called up, a pro rata basis is used to determine if that player is available.

A team is also allowed to request a postponement if both the first and second choice goalkeepers are called up too.

Players signed on loan also count.

As per Fifa's guidelines, players selected must be released by their clubs by the Monday morning ahead of the first international fixtures of that window.

For home clubs wishing to request a postponement, they must do so at least five days prior to the game they wish to postpone.

Away teams must submit a request seven days in advance.

title: Six-time Grand Slam champion Salisbury retires
description: Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury retires from professional tennis.
fullText:
Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury has retired from professional tennis.

Salisbury chose this month's US Open as his final event and reached the semi-finals with his long-time partner Rajeev Ram, who had also decided to retire.

The venue was fitting, as in 2023 Salisbury and Ram became the first pair in history to win three consecutive US Open men's doubles titles.

Salisbury is Britain's most successful men's doubles player of the Open Era. He also won the 2020 Australian Open with Ram, and two mixed doubles titles with Desirae Krawczyk.

The 34-year-old says he has been thinking about his future for a while, and is now "very happy with the decision."

"Tennis has been my life for as long as I can remember and I have been incredibly fortunate to have had all the opportunities, experiences and success that I have," he posted on Instagram.

"To be able to travel the world and call playing tennis my job has been a dream come true and I never believed I could have lived the life and had the career that I have.

"I gave it my all and know I can be proud and look back with no regrets."

Salisbury took a three month break at the start of this year, having told BBC Sport about the anxiety which had been affecting him on tour.

While he did not think it affected his tennis very much, he said it left him with a "feeling of dread" which made life on the road far less enjoyable.

Salisbury finishes his career with 17 tour level titles, including the season ending ATP Finals of 2022 and 2023.

fullText:
The first international break of the 2026/27 is almost upon us and it promises to be an unusual one, with FIFA introducing a three-week window during which national teams will play four games in a row.

For the European nations, those fixtures come in the UEFA Nations League, and new Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has responded in equally unusual fashion by naming a total of 44 players.

And, from Barcelona's perspective, their in-form forward Karim Adeyemi and loanee Marc-Andre ter Stegen, currently at AFC Ajax, have been called up by the new Germany head coach, however not in the same list.

Ter Stegen has been included in the first squad, while Adeyemi appears in the second.

As such, Ter Stegen will be available for Germany's matches against the Netherlands, coached by former Barcelona manager Xavi Hernandez, on 24 September, followed by Greece on 27 September.

Adeyemi will then join up for the games against Serbia on 1 October and Greece again on 4 October, this time away from home.

Only one player features in both selections: Augsburg goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.

Ter Stegen was left on the bench for Ajax's most recent match against Willem II, although that was due to rotation rather than a fitness issue.

With Germany, he is expected to take over as the team's first-choice goalkeeper following Manuel Neuer's retirement.

Adeyemi, meanwhile, had been left out of Germany's squad for the 2026 World Cup under Julian Nagelsmann. His performances since joining Barcelona have now opened the door to a return to international football.

title: Top Democrat places hold on Trump admin. plan to sell $2.8 billion in heavy bombs to Israel
description:
— The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Wednesday that he's going to block a proposed sale of $2.8 billion in heavy weaponry to Israel over concerns that the powerful bombs may not be used in line with U.S. and international law.
Rep.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Wednesday that he's going to block a proposed sale of $2.8 billion in heavy weaponry to Israel over concerns that the powerful bombs may not be used in line with U.S. and international law.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would withhold approval for the sale because of "grave, unresolved concerns" about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government.

"The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians," Meeks said in a statement. "I therefore will not clear this sale at this time."

Meeks' objections, however, will not likely affect the sale, which was informally notified to lawmakers on Tuesday. Once it is formally notified to Congress, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can bypass the normal congressional review process by making an emergency determination that the transaction is an urgent national security interest.

Rubio has done so in the past, including bypassing a normal congressional review process to approve a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel last year. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January.

The State Department did not respond to requests for comment about either the new proposed sale or Meeks' objection to it.

The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 powerful 2,000-pound bombs, The Associated Press has reported. The transfer of 2,000-pound bombs had been paused by the Biden administration over concerns about the possibility of mass casualties.

The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israel's military capacity and it comes as Israel is facing increased international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas.

The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The U.S. brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued.

description: World Cup-winning head coach Luis de la Fuente agrees a contract extension with Spain until 2032.
fullText:
World Cup-winning head coach Luis de la Fuente has agreed a contract extension with Spain until 2032.

The 65-year-old's previous deal was due to expire in 2028.

De la Fuente, who guided Spain to their fourth European Championship title in 2024 before securing global honours this summer, is now set to remain in charge for Spain's World Cup defence on home soil in 2030.

Spain will co-host the 24th edition of the men's World Cup alongside Portugal and Morocco, with a handful of matches scheduled for Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay as part of the competition's 100th anniversary celebrations.

De la Fuente succeeded Luis Enrique as head coach in December 2022, following Spain's last-16 exit at that year's World Cup.

Since then, they have lost just twice in 41 competitive matches and won three trophies, including the 2022-23 Uefa Nations League. They finished as runners-up to Portugal in 2024-25.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to lift their second men's World Cup crown in July, having defeated England 2-1 in the European showpiece two years earlier.

"His results speak for themselves, as does his work," said RFEF president Rafael Louzan, speaking at Wednesday's World Football Summit in Madrid.

"The public loves and admires him. I offered him an extension because he wasn't among the top 10 in terms of financial conditions. Now he will be.

"We're finalising the agreement so he can remain for several more years. He's been with us 14 years, and I want him to be able to finish his career here."

De la Fuente, who began his coaching career in Spain's lower leagues, spent nine years in Spain's youth set-up prior to replacing Luis Enrique, winning a European Under-19 Championship in 2015, a European Under-21 Championship in 2019 and a silver medal at the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo.
