title: How to Eat 'Healthy' in a World Full of Processed Food
description: Processed doesn't always mean unhealthy.
fullText:
Our world is full of processed food, for better or worse. It would be easy for me to sit at my keyboard and tell you to avoid it and eat foods in forms closest to how they are in nature: apples, not apple pie. But just because something is “processed” (whatever that means) doesn’t automatically make it bad for you. It’s time to lose the guilt and own up to eating processed food sometimes—and maybe we’ll see it’s not that bad.

Here’s the hard part: defining processed food. Doritos, processed. Not a tough call there. Raw potato with the dirt still on it: unprocessed. So far so good. But if we wash that potato, boil it, maybe peel it too...mix it with butter, and garlic (and then more butter, and more garlic)—uh-oh. That’s kind of processed, isn’t it? But it’s not very processed, you might say. There’s a spectrum, and if you dig a potato out of the ground and boil it in your own kitchen, that’s still on the okay side.

The problem comes when you try to draw a line to say these things are processed, and these things aren’t. Where would you put a cow that’s been chopped up into steaks? Vegetables that are frozen? Beans that are canned? Bread baked by a local baker? Bread baked by a factory?

It's a hard job, and no definition is going to make everyone happy. Probably the most popular is the NOVA framework for determining what's processed and what's "ultra processed." I wrote more about NOVA here, and why I think it's flawed. As a tool for studying food systems, it can be useful. But it doesn't tell us which foods are healthiest.

Sure, it takes a lot more work and machinery to process sugar than to harvest honeycomb and extract the honey, but that’s kind of beside the point of which is healthier for you. There is no major nutritional difference between the two. Taken to an extreme, the processed-is-bad mentality would put plenty of things off-limits that shouldn’t be. Frozen veggies are as healthy as fresh, sometimes more so. Pasteurized milk is processed, and better for it. There’s no solid nutritional reason to shun jarred pasta sauce, or egg whites in a carton, or rotisserie chicken. But wait, you say. Those are healthy processed foods. What about Twinkies? Doritos? McDonald’s? Hungry Man?

If some of the names in that list scared you, you probably have a reason why: sugar, or “chemicals” (we’re getting to that), or high-calorie portions, or high levels of fat. Before you decide that highly processed food is what you need to avoid, take a minute to consider what really matters to your health goals.

Here are the most common charges against processed foods, and how to steer clear of each:

They’re high in sugar, which most of us get too much of. This is easy to gauge if you check the label. There's a line item for sugars, but more importantly, since 2020 or so, there is also a line item for added sugars. That's the more important one to pay attention to.

They’re high in sodium. Many are: Highly processed foods are a bigger source of sodium in our diet than what we add in cooking or sprinkle with a salt shaker. Deli meats and restaurant meals are top sources. (For some reason, I keep hearing people say that soda has a lot of sodium. It doesn't—there's only 3% of your daily value in a bottle of Coke.) You can suss out sodium with its line item on the Nutrition Facts label.

They’re high in fat. This is true of oily snacks like chips, and often a lot of restaurant meals. Fat isn’t always a bad thing: It’s filling and arguably isn't as bad for you as sugar. Fat is listed on the Nutrition Facts label, along with its sub-categories saturated fat (probably not actually bad for you) and trans fat. Nobody likes trans fat, but it’s rapidly disappearing even from processed food.

They spike your blood sugar. High-carb foods that digest quickly can raise your blood sugar, which is not great if you're watching your glucose. (On the flip side, that's a good thing if you're an athlete looking for workout fuel.) Foods like Twizzlers and pretzels both fit the bill, for example. Anything that’s really heavy in fat, like potato chips, is actually lower on the glycemic index because the fat slows down digestion.

They’re addictive. There’s no label to check for this one, I’m afraid. Companies like to make money, so they’ll do what they can to make you want to come back for more. Some ready-to-eat junk foods, like chips and candy bars, are devilishly well-designed. A high-fat/high-sugar combo is the signature move, often with a good dose of salt thrown in. Basically, you can tell which foods these are because they’re the ones you have all the empty wrappers of at home.

They’re full of “chemicals.” Everything is made of chemicals, of course; chemistry is just the study of atoms and molecules. It’s true that some foods have long ingredient lists, and that many of the ingredients on them are hard to spell or pronounce. But there isn’t an association between how hard a name is to read and whether it refers to something dangerous. Heck, ascorbic acid and tocopherols are both used as preservatives, and look pretty mysterious on labels, but they’re just technical names for vitamin C and vitamin E. (They’re antioxidants in your body and in foods.) Colorings, flavorings, and preservatives aren’t automatically bad. Even those that have sparked controversy are still very likely to be safe.

They’re bad for the environment and/or economy. This is a “vote with your fork” (or, you know, orange-stained fingers) situation. If you don’t like buying from big companies and you’d rather give your money to the baker down the street than to the Nabisco corporation, by all means make that choice. Or maybe you object to the abundant plastic packaging and the carbon footprint of all the trucks that brought the ingredients to the processing plant and from the plant to you. Just keep those things clear in your mind: Food isn’t automatically unhealthy for your body just because its maker is greedy or wasteful.

With those factors in mind, you can now wander the aisles of the grocery store (or crunch the numbers for your favorite fast-food meal) with a better idea of what, if anything, you’re trying to avoid. If you’re trying to avoid sugar, for example, you might have to ditch that super healthy-looking agave-sweetened fruit drink, but you can chow down on all the pork rinds you want...if you’re into that sort of thing.

Now that you’ve got a plan, it’s time to figure out how to put it into place. If you often end up hungry at work when there’s nothing on hand besides the contents of a vending machine, you now have a way to evaluate what’s in that machine instead of writing off the whole thing as bad and wrong and terrible—and then feeling guilty when you get hungry enough that you give in and grab a Snickers.

For example, a pack of trail mix might be a good vending machine pick if you’re trying to avoid sugar, but it will be high in fat. At a gas station, a Lunchable might be hella processed, but it’s got protein and won’t send you into a carb coma—unlike, say, a pack of Pop-Tarts.

Of course, the best plan is to not need to buy any of that processed food. But how many of us can cook every meal from scratch? Here’s where it’s helpful to use some of those processed-but-still-healthy things we talked about earlier: the rotisserie chicken, for example. The frozen meatballs and jarred sauce to whip up a spaghetti dinner in minutes that will also become tomorrow’s lunch. You get the idea. I have some tips on starting to eat healthy here, and a guide here to meal prepping as a normal human who doesn't want to spend all weekend cooking.

It would be great to cook every meal from scratch, from lovingly foraged free-range lentils, but not all of us have time to do that. Sure, in some parts of history, people did—but that was part of their job as a housewife or farmer. Today, cooking every single meal from scratch is more like a hobby—a fine one to have, but not a mandate for everyone. We live in a world that’s full of processed food, and it’s totally okay to—carefully, thoughtfully—take advantage of that.

title: Magilton to remain in Cliftonville hot-seat
description: Jim Magilton will remain manager of Cliftonville despite Glentoran's interest in the former Northern Ireland international.
fullText:
Jim Magilton will remain manager of Cliftonville despite Glentoran's interest in the former Northern Ireland international.

The Glens are seeking a replacement for Declan Devine who left the Oval by mutual consent on Monday and had identified Magilton as a front-runner, making a formal approach to Cliftonville to speak to the Reds' boss.

However, Magilton will not made the switch to east Belfast and will remain in the Solitude dug-out when Cliftonville host the Glens in an Irish Premiership fixture on Saturday.

The 57-year-old former Northern Ireland international was appointed Cliftonville boss in 2023, succeeding Paddy McLaughlin, and led the club to Irish Cup glory the following year, ending a 45-year wait for the trophy.

Magilton, who previously worked at Ipswich Town, the Irish FA, Dundalk and Melbourne Victory, also led the Reds to the 2025 BetMcLean Cup, beating Glentoran in the final, but lost to Dungannon Swifts in the Irish Cup decider two months later.

Devine left the Oval club on Monday after two years in charge following a poor start to the season.

Assistant managers Paddy McCourt and Tim McCann oversaw Tuesday night's home defeat by Irish Premiership leaders Coleraine, and will now continue their search for Devine's replacement.

title: African greats inspired by the potential of Nairobi 2029
description: Some of Africa's great track and field stars expect the decision to award Kenya the 2029 World Athletics Championships to inspire the next generation.
fullText:
The decision to award the 2029 World Athletics Championships to Nairobi has prompted an outpouring of celebration across Africa.

Ethiopian great Haile Gebrselassie, a two-time Olympic 10,000m champion, congratulated the whole continent on the "wonderful news" following the announcement by World Athletics on Tuesday morning.

The Kenyan capital saw off former Olympic Games hosts London and Rome to secure a slice of history, with the event set to be held in Africa for the first time.

Unsurprisingly, news that the globe's top athletes will descend on the 48,000-capacity Kasarani Stadium in three years' time has gone down well with some of East Africa's biggest track and field stars.

Given the passionate following the sport has in Kenya, several commenters have stated that athletics will be "coming home".

Julius Yego, javelin world champion in 2015, said winning the bid is "a huge thing for Africa".

"I'm so happy that the world will come to Kenya," the 37-year-old told the BBC World Service.

"Africa has produced the best of athletes but we've never had a chance to witness such a big championship.

"It is something that will bring people to Africa. And people will know Africa."

Kenyans are known for their love of athletics, with 68% of people from the country who were surveyed by World Athletics rating their interest in the sport as high.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships

Kenya to host 2029 World Athletics Championships in African first

Gebrselassie expects the atmosphere inside the Kasarani Stadium, which is undergoing redevelopment ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, to be "very different".

"This is something very big in front of your people, in front of your city," he said.

"Many spectators can fly to Nairobi, many people can watch their athletes.

"It's going to be wonderful. I myself will be there to watch.

"Like in soccer, playing at home and then playing [away] is different. It's a big chance for Kenyans, it's a big chance for Ethiopians, in 2029, to win a race."

Janeth Jepkosgei, who won the women's 800m title at the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, thinks the "really exciting" decision will inspire the next generation of athletes.

"It means a lot for the youth and the juniors because it makes the dream really big," she said.

"This is the time where the youth and juniors should begin dreaming of winning at home."

Jepkosgei, who has moved into coaching since retiring from competition, says aspiring stars now have a very firm target in mind after being given a chance to challenge for world titles on home soil.

"We have been dreaming with these young ones, setting their goals," she said.

"This is where the young ones we have now can showcase their talent.

"Because we have three years [for] those athletes who are really promising. It is a good way to make them stay dedicated to it, focused and disciplined to the event.

"I've been speaking to my athletes and they're saying 'It has come home, we have to be there, on that starting line'."

Kenyan sprinter Ferdinand Omanyala, the holder of the African 100m record, was himself inspired by Nairobi hosting the Under-18 World Championships in 2017.

The 30-year-old expects the 2029 event to give a "big boost" to both current athletes and the generations to come.

"I can imagine what this is going to do to up-and-coming athletes," he said.

"They're going to see all these stars coming into the country and they'll be having this chance to watch them warm up and compete. That will be a huge motivation."

Africa will stage several big events over the next four years, with the first of those the upcoming Youth Olympics in the Senegalese capital Dakar from 31 October to 13 November.

South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia will host next year's men's Cricket World Cup, while the men's Fifa World Cup will return to the continent for the first time since 2010 when Morocco co-hosts alongside Spain and Portugal in 2030.

Yego feels the landmark of seeing athletics' flagship competition on African soil should give the rest of the continent belief in their abilities to put on major events.

"As Africans, we need to think big and plan ahead and think 'Yes, it is possible for Africa to host a championship like the World Championships'.

"Same of course for the Olympics. Africa hosted the World Cup in 2010 in South Africa, so I think we're capable of hosting big events.

"Let's dream of hosting the Olympics and bring the best of the world in sports to Africa - to feel Africa, to enjoy Africa."

Both Egypt and South Africa have previously said they want to host the 2036 Olympics.

Yego's positive view is shared by Gebrselassie, who also hopes other cities will gain the confidence to bid for global events.

"This is a big chance, not only in sport, in economy, politics. Now Africans can do anything they want," the 53-year-old said.

"If Nairobi can host this championship, why not Addis Ababa? Why not Lagos or South Africa, Uganda, Rwanda?

"In 2029, I think the whole world will be surprised at how well they (Kenya) host."

title: England's Hardcastle announces international retirement
description: England women's all-time record try scorer Amy Hardcastle announces her international retirement.
fullText:
England women's all-time record try scorer Amy Hardcastle has announced her international retirement.

The St Helens centre, 37, scored 30 tries in 29 appearances for her country, having made her international debut in 2009.

England head coach Stuart Barrow described her as "one of the defining players of her generation".

She leaves the international game a month before the start of the Rugby League World Cup - having featured at the past three tournaments - but will continue to play at club level.

Hardcastle was the only England player selected in the Women's Team of the Decade, picked by the NRL in 2020 to highlight the outstanding players of the 2010s.

"Representing England has been the greatest honour of my rugby league career," she said.

"To wear the national shirt, play alongside so many incredible team-mates and represent my family, clubs and community has meant everything to me.

"After a lot of reflection, I feel now is the right time to step away from the international game. I'm incredibly proud of what we've achieved and how far women's rugby league has come during my career.

"I'd like to thank every coach, team-mate, member of staff and supporter who has been part of my international journey.

"I'll be the biggest cheerleader for the girls who are selected to fly to Australia, and I wish the squad and Stuart Barrow every success at the Rugby League World Cup."

England's opening match of the World Cup is against Wales in Perth on 17 October.

Paying tribute to Hardcastle, England head coach Barrow added: "She has been an outstanding ambassador for the sport, a role model for young players and someone who has consistently driven standards on and off the field.

"Throughout her international career, Amy has shown professionalism, resilience and an unwavering commitment to the England programme.

"She has performed on the biggest stages, inspired team-mates and helped elevate the profile of women's rugby league both nationally and internationally."

title: Verstappen passes 100 amateur karters in 14 laps in exhibition race
description: Four-time F1 world champion Max Verstappen passes 100 amateur drivers in just 14 laps in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.
fullText:
Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.

The four-time Formula 1 world champion had a maximum of 35 laps and 75 minutes to pass everyone on an adapted track at the grand prix circuit in Northamptonshire.

Red Bull's Verstappen, 28, was up to 37th by the end of a chaotic first lap in which many drivers crashed or span out, resulting in racing being briefly suspended.

The ruthless Dutchman, who warned participants "it's not a charity event" on race radio, moved into 10th by the start of lap six and was in fourth by lap 10, with each driver who he passed having to retire.

At that stage, the field - made up of TV, sport and social media personalities, with no professional racing drivers - consisted of just Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, Red Bull engine builder Lewis Osler and YouTuber Zac Alsop.

All three were given an extra 'fast lap' where they could cut a corner of the track to try to hold off Verstappen for longer, but he inevitably reeled them in.

Martens, who was on pole position after qualifying, was the final driver to be passed as Verstappen completed his challenge with 40 minutes and 21 laps to spare.

Verstappen began his racing career as a junior in karting and won four consecutive F1 titles between 2021 and 2024.

A return to the places that shaped an unforgettable chapter of his story. Lothar Matthäus was back in the world of Inter, revisiting the places at the heart of his Nerazzurri journey: Inter HQ, San Siro and the Inter Training Center in Appiano Gentile. It was a journey through memories and emotions, celebrating a bond with the Nerazzurri colours that has stood the test of time.

A Ballon d'Or winner, Italian champion and leader in one of the greatest Inter sides of all time, Matthäus left an indelible mark on the Club's history. After arriving in Milano in 1988, the German midfielder played a starring role in the record-breaking Scudetto triumph of 1988/89 and helped Inter achieve further success during that era. Many years on, his bond with Inter remains as strong as ever, with San Siro and the Nerazzurri world at the heart of so many cherished memories.

The journey began on the evening of 14 September, when Matthäus returned to San Siro to watch Chivu's side come from behind to beat Udinese 5-3 in a thrilling encounter. His return was celebrated before kick-off, as Lothar stepped back onto the pitch where he once worked his magic before taking his place in the stands at the stadium where he wrote some of the most memorable chapters of his career in an Inter shirt.

The following morning, on 15 September, Matthäus visited Inter HQ, where he immersed himself in the Club's history and spent time in the trophy room. Surrounded by trophies, memorabilia and historic photographs, the former midfielder looked back on the seasons he spent in Nerazzurri colours.

The journey then continued at San Siro, where Matthäus enjoyed the spectacular Skywalk experience. From high above the Meazza, Matthäus was able to look down once again on the stage where he achieved some of his most legendary feats in an Inter shirt.

The final stop was the Inter Training Center, where Matthäus connected with the Inter of today while reliving the emotions and memories of his own Nerazzurri journey. It was a chance to rediscover the meaning of colours that remain part of his story to this day.

title: ‘If you’re building Frankenstein, stop’: JD Vance dismisses calls for AI regulation

fullText:
US vice-president’s comments come as former Anthropic researcher revisits recent claim AI could destroy humanity

The US vice-president has dismissed calls for global regulation of AI safety risks, telling companies creating the most advanced models: “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop.”

In remarks addressed towards Dario Amodei, the co-founder of Anthropic who has called on Washington DC to coordinate control of AI systems, including with China, JD Vance said: “If you’re gonna create Frankenstein, don’t come to the government and say we need regulation.”

He said tech bosses should instead: “Look inward and accept that if you’re building Frankenstein, No 1, you should stop and No 2, when companies come to you and say: ‘We need the tools to fight back against Frankenstein,’ give them those tools.”

Vance was speaking at an AI summit in Los Angeles after a week of rising global concern at the risks to humanity posed by the prospect of the creation of an artificial superintelligence, a technology that does not yet exist.

Amodei on Saturday warned that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months.

Although many doubt that claim, it added fuel to the suggestion from Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, that there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within 10 years. He was responding to a researcher, Jacob Coxon, who quit Anthropic with a similar warning.

On Tuesday night, Coxon gave an amended prognosis: “I do think that if we go slower we can take risk to 0%, but this requires radical action.” He also admitted “it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios” in which AI kills all humans and said: “I need to work on communicating this point.”

Vance’s willingness to consider that AI could pose a real risk marked a split from the US president, Donald Trump, who wrote this week: “AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Trump posted on social media that AI is going to be “the greatest economic development engine in history – bigger than oil, gold, diamonds, or even the internet”.

Vance has said he suspects AI leaders of raising the alarm about safety risks as a “Trojan horse”. Amodei has proposed industry coordination to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” while US and global regulation is implemented. Critics of the companies believe they are encouraging the US government to create tough new rules – shaped in their interests – that could limit wider competition in a tactic known as regulatory capture.

OpenAI, which lost control of hundreds of AI agents during testing this summer which then conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website, said on Monday it was backing bipartisan efforts by lawmakers in Washington to address catastrophic risks from AI and it has been coordinating with Google and Anthropic.

On Wednesday, Reuters reported claims from an independent researcher, Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, that OpenAI’s rogue agents had started probing Hugging Face for weaknesses nearly two months before the attack.

Sam Altman, the Chat GPT-maker’s chief executive, on Tuesday criticised suggestions from other companies that “we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible”. Altman said: “There should be no qualifier on that.”

Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and chief executive of Meta, advocated that companies should take unilateral safety action. He said his company had recently delayed the release of its most recent AI model, Muse, “for several months to focus on safety and security”.

“We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

Meta has been forced to pay out billions in legal cases related to harms caused by its social media platforms. Last month it settled a case with US states claiming Facebook and Instagram harmed children by agreeing to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn).

Zuckerberg stressed: “[AI] labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”

title: Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous proposition

fullText:
Tech CEOs banding together is an old ruse recycled from corporate America to get a pass from antitrust laws

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome.

The safety breach disclosed by OpenAI after a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed.

The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industry have warned. These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses.

It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what other fantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being.

Amodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal.

“Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens when OpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?”

As Bill Gates has written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not.

The argument that excessive competition is driving a race to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation to child labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools.

Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes from

Amodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks. The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety.

But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic. Tremors in capital markets suggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy.

Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”.

So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI.

Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms.

On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not been inadvertently rewarded for misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line.

In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension.

There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.

title: Why is Brinker International stock gaining today?
As price of fuel ratchets up, so does anger of people who can no longer afford it
description: Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the war in Iran drives up the cost of energy.
fullText:
Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the now monthslong US war with Iran drives up the cost of energy globally.

Oil prices climbed back above the $100 per barrel mark last week in the wake of further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf and reignited fighting in Yemen that threatens shipping in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

For the United States, that has meant elevated gas prices and stark warnings for households that rely on heating oil to keep warm in the winter, as analysts forecast a 30% jump in prices amid the Iran war.

For less wealthy nations, the hit to their national finances – and people's wallets – has been even starker with patience often running out.

As the price of fuel ratchets up, so does the anger of people who can no longer afford to pay for gas, get to work, run their businesses or even carry out essential services.

In Syria, protesters burned tires on a busy highway. In Guatemala, they blocked roads to demand immediate government action. And in Portugal, local business leaders and workers marched to the prime minister's home.

Here's a closer look at the protests and the global impacts of sky-high energy costs:

A steep rise in fuel prices over the weekend ignited protests across Syria, marking the largest demonstrations in the country since the fall of the Assad regime two years ago.

The country's government temporarily raised diesel prices to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43) a liter – roughly a 40% hike – according to Syrian news agency SANA. It also raised prices for gas by more than 25%.

The Syrian Energy Ministry has said the steep price increases are due to surging global fuel prices and ongoing maintenance at the country's largest refinery, Baniyas, which has increased its reliance on imports, SANA reported.

While dozens of protests have been peaceful, demonstrators on Sunday blocked the Hasaka–Deir ez-Zor highway, where they burned tires and stopped oil tankers, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.

"Fuel availability, rising prices, falling purchasing power, and poor services are all reasons that have accumulated public resentment, although demands are also shifting toward reversing decisions and removing officials, including the energy minister, showing that economic grievances are turning into grievances against the government," said Muaz Al Abdullah, a Syria analyst at ACLED.

Video filmed by Reuters news agency from the scene of a protest in Aleppo on Sunday shows people burning tires and shouting chants criticizing the governments' fuel hike decision.

"All those present here want a reduction in diesel prices. We don't want higher wages, we want cheaper (fuel)," one Syrian protester, Yasser Salim, told Reuters.

Another protester, Bassam al-Ali, said: "We do not want roundabouts, every day they (the government) build a new roundabout that costs a million thousand dollars, and malls and I don't know what … Your people were with you, is still with you now and will remain with you – but this will let things explode."

Last week in Guatemala, groups of organized truckers and other protesters blocked highways and caused damage in various parts of the country to protest rising fuel prices, according to the Associated Press.

Other videos taken by local media show people marching peacefully through Guatemala City to demand immediate government action.

The country's Congress is now working to address the widespread discontent through a proposed law that would cap prices until the end of the year, but the bill is still making its way through the legislative process, according to Guatemala's national news agency AGN. If passed, it would mean that a government subsidy is paid to fuel importers if prices exceed the established cap, according to AP.

"This is an issue that must be resolved as a country. The executive, the legislative, and everyone else involved must resolve it. People cannot pay these prices and not feel the impact on their finances," said the president of the Congress, Luis Contreras Colindres, in an address on Monday.

"Diesel is the engine that drives this country's economy," Contreras said, according to AGN.

Protests took place in the coastal city of Espinho, Portugal, on Saturday to protest both rising gas prices and the soaring cost of living.

About 80 people took part in that demonstration, which was organized by local business leaders and aimed at pressuring the government to find solutions, according to Portugal's Lusa News Agency. The protesters marched until they reached the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in Espinho.

Meanwhile, the Portuguese Firefighters' League (LBP) has sounded the alarm that surging fuel prices are becoming unsustainable for fire brigades and saddling volunteer organizations with costs they can't keep up with.

On Monday, the country's government announced a new package of measures intended to ease the fuel price crunch, according to Lusa. Those measures include support for freight transporters, taxi drivers, the fire service and the social sector, the news agency reported.

About 50 fishermen blockaded a major fuel depot in the coastal southern French town of Fos-sur-Mer on Tuesday, in part to protest rising fuel prices, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV.

The blockade lasted several hours and the protesters briefly clashed with police, BFMTV reported.

Mayor Philippe Maurizot said the fishing industry in the town is facing a "profound crisis that demands an urgent and strong response from the state," and said the protesters' anger "must be heard."

"Rising costs, increased fuel prices, a growing number of constraints, insufficient income, and a lack of visibility are placing some professionals in an untenable situation," he said in the letter addressed to the French prime minister.

Workers of the Philippine transport group Manibela went on strike on Monday to protest fuel price hikes – calling for government subsidies and scrapped fuel taxes.

It comes as petroleum companies in the country announced another round of fuel price hikes, which went into effect on Tuesday, hitting drivers with an increase of 5.68 pesos (0.01) per liter of gas, according to the Philippine News Agency (PNA). The prices of diesel and kerosene were also hiked again this week, according to PNA.

"We know that every increase at the pump affects more than the cost of filling up a vehicle. It affects the daily budget of families, the livelihood of our drivers, and the operating costs of businesses," said Energy Secretary Energy Secretary Sharon S. Garin, as she announced on Tuesday that the government had cleared a hurdle to potentially reduce excise taxes on petroleum products.

Bus drivers and motorists have been struggling for months amid the rising costs, which surged drastically in March and still remain elevated compared to pre-war prices.

Back in March at the height of the country's fuel crisis – about a month after the start of the Iran war – people in Manila marched toward the country's presidential palace to express discontent with steeply rising energy prices.

"The Philippines should stand up and call for an end to the US aggression against Iran. The impact of the oil disruption affects us all. We might not have been hit by bombs, but we are being hit by poverty and hunger because of the rise in oil prices," said trade union leader Jerome Adonis in late March.

Student unions have also joined the widespread protests at various points this year, railing against a wider cost of living crisis in the Philippines.

CNN's Heather Law contributed to this report.

The DP World Tour's 2027 schedule - which features 42 tournaments in 24 countries - will also include three returning events with the Hong Kong Open, the Singapore Open and Open de Portugal.

title: Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
description: Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
fullText:
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.

Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.

They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.

"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."

The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.

And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.

They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.

"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."

Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."

Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.

There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.

And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.

"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."

And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."

The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.

And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.

"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."

The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.

Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.

"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

title: What's gone wrong for Chelsea talent Kendry Paez?
description: Kendry Paez was one of the world's best young talents when Chelsea signed him as a 16-year-old. Three years later, he's playing for the Under-21s. So what has gone wrong?
fullText:
Attacking midfielder Kendry Paez has finally pulled on a Chelsea shirt, three years after agreeing a move to Stamford Bridge - albeit for the club's Under-21s.

Chelsea agreed a £17.27m deal to sign Paez from Ecuadorian side Independiente del Valle in 2023 when he was 16, but his development has not progressed as quickly as many expected.

Now 19, Paez made his first appearance in Chelsea colours for Cobham Next Gen, the club's newly-renamed Under-21 side, as a 12th-minute substitute in a 4-1 win away to Arsenal on Saturday.

It comes after new manager Xabi Alonso said the midfielder was "not in my plans" and Chelsea listed him as an academy player on the club website.

Chelsea explored the possibility of a loan move in English football, but Fifa regulations left the club unable to send him overseas after using all six of their available international loan slots.

With 27 caps for Ecuador, an appearance at this summer's World Cup and a reputation as one of South America's brightest young talents alongside Blues team-mate Estevao Willian, what has happened to Paez?

Paez is a record breaker and a headline maker.

He became the youngest debutant and goalscorer in Ecuadorian top-flight history at the age of 15 before making his debut in the Copa Libertadores, South America's equivalent of the Champions League, later that same season.

Later in 2023, aged 16 years and 131 days, he made his second appearance for Ecuador, becoming the second-youngest South American international to feature in World Cup qualifying after Diego Maradona.

A month later, he became the youngest South American to score in a World Cup qualifier in a 2-1 win away to Bolivia.

It was understandable, therefore, that Chelsea believed the attacker, who had two international goals and 18 caps when they agreed to sign him, was destined for big things.

Chelsea allowed him to train regularly with the first team before he was officially eligible to join the club following his 18th birthday.

They also provided security for Paez, his family and the family of international team-mate Moises Caicedo after violence broke out in Ecuador in early 2024.

A few months later, Paez was filmed in a New York strip club while away on international duty.

He initially impressed on loan at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg by winning September's Young Player of the Month award in the French top flight, but then came in for criticism from then-manager Liam Rosenior.

"We expect more, clearly," Rosenior said later that season. "I'm tired of using the excuse of the player's youth."

Despite Strasbourg's links to Chelsea through their shared ownership, the loan was cut short after one goal in 21 appearances. Instead, he joined Argentine giants River Plate on a two-year loan spell.

Sources in Argentina expressed similar concerns about his attitude when asked by BBC Sport. They point to a disappointing display in the 1-0 Superclasico defeat by fierce rivals Boca Juniors at the Monumental in April.

Shortly afterwards, Paez was named by club president Stefano Di Carlo as one of 15 players training away from River Plate's first team, although other sources felt he could have been given more opportunities.

His loan ended by mutual consent after Paez scored once in 14 appearances in 461 minutes for River Plate.

Ahead of the international break, concern has been expressed in Ecuador, having built him up as the country's next great attacking talent.

Michel Deller, the owner of Independiente, told Hincha Amarillo: "He's like a son to us. We care about him deeply.

"He's a good kid who's had a tough time and has made decisions that have complicated his life.

"We are always hopeful he'll show his exceptional talent one again but right now, it's up to him to decide what to do with his life."

These concerns are not dismissed completely by Chelsea or Paez's environment. However, there is a belief they are grossly overstated, highlighting he is owed time to grow as a player and person.

There was one reminder of Paez's quality in the dying moments of Cobham Next Gen's (Chelsea Under-21s) defeat at Wycombe Wanderers in the EFL Trophy on Tuesday.

It was an outswinging cross from a short corner routine, which Harrison Bettoni tapped in during added time. He then put in another cross that caused havoc as Chelsea chased an equaliser in front of just 778 fans.

It was a much-needed boost for Spanish-speaking Paez, who appeared to stand alone from the other academy players before kick-off.

He did join in their warm-ups but mostly kept to himself before coming on in the 62nd minute.

Ultimately Chelsea lost, while Paez was a peripheral figure playing as a right-sided No 10, like Cole Palmer, in a system that mirrored Alonso's back-three shape.

That was until his flurry of activity late on.

Although he's not Chelsea's youngest player, Paez has already made 70 appearances for Ecuadorian side Independiente and more than 100 senior matches in total.

It's something he can fall back on in a more than salvageable situation.

Chelsea have been encouraged by his attitude, having him back in the building at Cobham where he has trained in a stable and elite environment.

There is stability around him as family attended his recent match at Wycombe.

The Blues are also now able to monitor his development more closely, while academy matches are regularly attended by scouts from across the English Football League and beyond.

There is optimism from those close to Paez that he can impress and gain a first loan move in England in January, or one of the six international loan spots will become available for him to go overseas again.

It's more than possible he can rediscover the form that attracted Chelsea in the first place and fulfil the immense potential that made him one of South America's most coveted young talents.

title: Fitzpatrick not '100% comfortable' with tour finals in Dubai
description: Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.
fullText:
Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.

Fitzpatrick is concerned that the United Arab Emirates could be a target in the ongoing conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel.

"You've only got to look at the hotel that got hit earlier this year," Fitzpatrick told BBC Sport. "I was having dinner the week I won in that hotel.

"That's obviously very scary when you think about how it was a few months away but how close you were to that particular spot and for something like that to happen. It's obviously quite scary."

Fitzpatrick would like to see the event switched to a different host country, a decision he called a "no brainer, in my opinion" before adding: "But I'm not a sponsor, I'm not paying the bills and all that sort of stuff.

"I'm sure there's more to it than just the meets the eye."

Led by chief executive Guy Kinnings, DP World Tour officials are assessing safety issues for their final two play-off events in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai.

Both tournaments are backed by key sponsors of the European-based tour and provide a lucrative end to the season for the circuit's leading money winners.

"I think it's annoying, but at the same time, Guy Kinnings can't control what Iran are doing," Fitzpatrick added.

"It is frustrating because as someone who likes to plan and be prepared, it is difficult to kind of figure out what's going on. Obviously, things as they stand are a bit weird over there.

"I can't say I'm like 100% comfortable, but I guess you just have to see nearer the time and, you know, I still need to qualify as well."

Fitzpatrick's Ryder Cup team-mate Shane Lowry said the tour faces important choices over how to end the current season. "They are huge decisions for everyone," said last week's winner of the Irish Open.

"I'm not going to sit here and comment on the whole thing because I think it's up to the powers above to sort that all out. I think if the tournaments are on, the players are going to go. And if they are not, they will find an alternative."

A spokesperson for the DP World Tour said: "We are in constant dialogue with our members and their management teams about the tournaments they play in, but ultimately players' individual schedule choices are a matter for them to decide.

"As far as our play-offs are concerned, it remains our intention to play as scheduled in the UAE but we continue to monitor the situation and take advice from our international travel advisors."

title: F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco
description: Formula 1 increases the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 World Championship.
fullText:
Formula 1 has increased the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 World Championship.

Sprint events, which feature a shorter race on Saturday and an extra qualifying session on Friday, will be held for the first time in Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi.

The other sprints will be in Canada, Britain, Italy, Brazil, and Qatar, it was revealed as the calendar was formally announced.

The maximum number of sprints previously in a season has been six.

The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, followed by Saudi Arabia a week later, but both events will remain in doubt while the war in the Middle East continues.

Bahrain is the default season-opening race, but Australia has hosted the first grand prix for the past two years because of the timing of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan.

The 2026 season is due to end with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and while F1 is planning to complete the calendar as scheduled, it is working on contingency plans if those races cannot be held as a result of the continuing conflict between the US/Israel and Iran.

The same applies for the start of next season as F1 considers its options for an alternative opening schedule if racing in the Middle East looks impossible by the end of this year.

On Sunday, a summit involving some of the nations involved in or affected by the conflict released a statement urging "maximum restraint" in the war.

The British Grand Prix will be on 2-4 July, and the 2027 season re-introduces races in Portugal and Turkey, returning for the first time since being used as placeholder events during the pandemic.

Sprint events usually come at a higher price for race organisers but they are in demand because they increase the chance of selling more tickets, with competitive action on each of the three days of the meeting rather than only Saturday and Sunday.

Silverstone believe holding a sprint this year was a large part of the reason for the British Grand Prix’s highest ever attendance - 64,000 more fans attended over the course of the four days compared with the year before, which was not a sprint.

The inclusion of a sprint event in Monaco will inevitably raise eyebrows, given it is almost impossible to overtake around the historic street circuit.

However, F1 is selling it on the fact that it means there will be two qualifying sessions at Monaco - qualifying around the demanding track is renowned as one of the highlights of the season.

Two separate qualifying sessions could also provide two different grid orders, increasing variability.

The flip side of a sprint in Monaco is that, because of the lack of overtaking opportunities, the finishing order of the sprint will be pretty much locked in once the cars have completed the first lap, barring accidents.

F1 president and chief executive officer Stefano Domenicali said: "We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Turkey to the championship and to expand sprint racing to 10 events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special."

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of F1's governing body the FIA, said: "The 2027 FIA F1 World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport.

"With 24 grands prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Turkey, and the opportunity for an expanded sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards."

Pre-season testing is also scheduled to be held in Bahrain on 24-27 February.

title: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, says he’s living in an Airstream trailer to oversee xAI’s biggest expansion yet
description: Musk says he is living at xAI’s Memphis data center site, continuing a longtime habit of sleeping where he works.
fullText:
Elon Musk, the world's richest man, has some new digs—an Airstream trailer in Memphis, parked just steps from xAI's most ambitious project yet.

Musk, who has a net worth of $917 billion according to the Bloomberg Billionaire Index and became the world's first trillionaire for 12 days in June, said Monday he was in his new "palace" as he spoke during a taping of the All-In podcast alongside Gwynne Shotwell, the president and chief operating officer of SpaceX.

Shotwell, for her part, praised Musk's latest unusual home as an example of his long history of committing fully to projects he cares about throughout his career.

"This is Elon, by the way, doing what people don't believe he does. He sleeps on the factory floor. He's in Memphis, helping build buildings," she said during the interview.

Musk is in Memphis as xAI races to expand Colossus, a massive supercomputer center that has provided it with so much computing power that it has struck deals to provide excess capacity to Google and Anthropic for billions. The company started building Colossus in 2024 to provide compute for Grok, xAI's large language model, and the initial build reportedly took only 122 days.

While putting a data center in space could still be far off, Memphis has emerged as the center of xAI's infrastructure buildout here on Earth. In late July, the company announced it would build a fourth data center called Minihard that will add to its other facilities.

Musk did not say which Airstream model he was living in, but some of the aluminum-shelled campers pack a sleeping area, kitchen, and bathroom into a 16-foot space.

Still, Musk has been known to want to sleep close to the action when a new project interested him or required his direct attention. When Musk and his brother Kimbal were building their first startup, Zip2, in the '90s, they slept in a tiny Palo Alto office for six months while showering at the YMCA, according to Walter Isaacson's biography of Musk.

Even as a newfound multi-millionaire, having received $22 million from selling Zip2 to Compaq, Musk slept under his desk most nights as he prepared to launch X.com, the online bank that would later become PayPal, in 1999, according to Isaacson's biography.

Even when he rose to the rank of super wealthy, having received another approximately $175 million from eBay's acquisition of PayPal, he often stayed at colleagues' homes while traveling in Silicon Valley, including the home of Michael Marks, who briefly served as Tesla CEO in 2007 before the pair clashed and Musk later took over the role.

title: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears in court in The Hague
description: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing charges of crimes against humanity at the International Criminal Court, made his first public appearance in more than a year on Wednesday, wh...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing charges of crimes against humanity at the International Criminal Court, made his first public appearance in more than a year on Wednesday, when he attended a pretrial hearing at the court in The Hague.

The 81-year old is accused of murder and attempted murder for his alleged involvement in dozens of killings as part of his so-called war on drugs while in office, first as the mayor of a southern city in the Philippines and later as president. He denies the charges against him.

He has missed a series of hearings since his arrest in 2025. Medical reasons were cited for his absence but the court's judges ruled in January that he was healthy enough to stand trial.

The presiding judge in his case told Duterte's legal team during an earlier hearing that she wanted the ex-leader to attend Wednesday's session.

"We would expect Mr. Duterte to be here unless there's some medical issue," Judge Joanna Korner said during the June pretrial hearing.

Wednesday's hearing is to discuss evidence disclosure and come up with a timetable for the trial, which is due to open in November.

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 and was set to appear in court in The Hague in September last year. However, the hearing was delayed after a pretrial panel of judges granted a "limited postponement" to give the court time to determine whether Duterte was fit enough to take part in the proceedings.

Following an assessment by a panel of medical experts, judges ruled that Duterte is "fit to take part in the pretrial proceedings."

The ICC has been looking into mass killings in crackdowns overseen by Duterte since 2018. Estimates of the death toll during Duterte's presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 that the national police have reported up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups.

According to the prosecutors, police and government hit squads carried out dozens of killings at Duterte's orders, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.

A month after the court in February 2018 announced a preliminary investigation into the violent drug crackdowns, Duterte said the Philippines would withdraw from the ICC.

Last year, judges rejected a request from Duterte's legal team to throw out the case because of the Philippine withdrawal. Countries cannot "abuse" their right to withdraw from the court's foundational Rome Statute "by shielding persons from justice in relation to alleged crimes that are already under consideration," the decision says.

Earlier this year, an attempt by authorities to arrest another man wanted by the ICC in connection with the drug killings dissolved into gunfire in the Philippine Senate in May. No one was hurt. The court had unsealed an arrest warrant for Ronald Marapon dela Rosa, who served as national police chief under Duterte. Dela Rosa went into hiding following the Senate standoff and remains on the run.

Two months later, the Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened the trial of Duterte's daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte. If convicted of the charges, which include amassing unexplained wealth and publicly threatening the family of the current president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., she may be permanently disqualified from holding public office. She denies the charges.

title: Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
description: Argentina name Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
fullText:
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.

Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".

Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.

"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.

River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.

Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

Argentina were ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, although one match of that sanction was suspended, for breaches of the Fifa disciplinary code during the World Cup.

The punishment related to using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.

After defeating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner claiming Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory.

As they play friendlies against Bolivia on 30 September in Cordoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October, it should mean the punishment will have been served before the Benin game.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes and team-mate Nahuel Molina are not expected to be available as they were given respective 10-game and seven-match suspensions for their part in on-field clashes following their country's defeat by Spain in the World Cup final.
